**Nísia Verônica Trindade Lima** [GCRB](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordem_de_Rio_Branco "Ordem de Rio Branco") • [GCMD](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordem_do_Mérito_da_Defesa "Ordem do Mérito da Defesa") ([Rio de Janeiro](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro "Rio de Janeiro"), [17 de janeiro](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/17_de_janeiro "17 de janeiro") de [1958](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/1958 "1958")) é uma sanitarista, [cientista social](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ciências_sociais "Ciências sociais"), [socióloga](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociologia "Sociologia"), [pesquisadora](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pesquisa "Pesquisa") e [professora universitária](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professor_catedrático "Professor catedrático") [brasileira](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brasileiros "Brasileiros") filiada ao [Partido dos Trabalhadores](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partido_dos_Trabalhadores "Partido dos Trabalhadores") (PT).[[1]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-1) Em [2026](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleições_gerais_no_Brasil_em_2026 "Eleições gerais no Brasil em 2026"), foi eleita [deputada federal](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputado_federal "Deputado federal") pelo [Rio de Janeiro](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro_(estado) "Rio de Janeiro (estado)").[[2]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-2)

Membro titular da [Academia Brasileira de Ciências](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academia_Brasileira_de_Ciências "Academia Brasileira de Ciências")[[3]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-ABC-3), Foi [ministra da Saúde](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lista_de_ministros_da_Saúde_do_Brasil "Lista de ministros da Saúde do Brasil") do [Brasil](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brasil "Brasil") no [governo Lula III](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governo_Lula_(2023–presente) "Governo Lula (2023–presente)") entre 2023 e 2025 e presidente da [Fundação Oswaldo Cruz](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundação_Oswaldo_Cruz "Fundação Oswaldo Cruz") entre 2017 e 2022, tendo sido a primeira mulher a presidir a instituição.[[4]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-:0-4)[[5]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-fiocruz-5)

## Biografia

Filha de Nivaldo de Assis Lima, seu pai nasceu em 20 de agosto de 1925, em [Condeúba](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condeúba "Condeúba"), vindo a falecer em 6 de novembro de 2023 aos 98 anos de idade. Ele era filho de Gustavo Fagundes de Lima (tio do poeta [Camillo de Jesus Lima](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camillo_de_Jesus_Lima "Camillo de Jesus Lima")), fez o curso ginasial em [Vitória da Conquista](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitória_da_Conquista "Vitória da Conquista") e se formou em direito na Universidade do Rio de Janeiro. Seu pai foi juiz de direito substituto da Comarca de [Paracambi](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paracambi "Paracambi"), professor de português e literatura, poeta, cronista e epigramista, morava em [Santo André](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santo_André_(São_Paulo) "Santo André (São Paulo)").[[6]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-6) Ele foi responsável por lhe contar as primeiras histórias sobre o Brasil, sobre sua literatura e potencial da mesma para a transformação social.[[7]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-iesp-7)[[8]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-portal-8)

Nísia nasceu no [Rio de Janeiro](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro "Rio de Janeiro"), em 1958, crescendo no [bairro do Flamengo](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flamengo_(bairro_do_Rio_de_Janeiro) "Flamengo (bairro do Rio de Janeiro)"). Por inspiração de uma professora de [sociologia](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociologia "Sociologia") durante o ensino médio, Nísia decidiu cursar Ciências Sociais, pela [Universidade do Estado do Rio de Janeiro](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universidade_do_Estado_do_Rio_de_Janeiro "Universidade do Estado do Rio de Janeiro") (UERJ), em 1976.[[7]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-iesp-7)[[8]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-portal-8)

Envolvida, na graduação, ao movimento estudantil pró-democracia, participou da construção do centro acadêmico de Ciências Humanas da universidade. Ao se formar, ingressou como professora na rede estadual e particular da cidade. Em 1982, iniciou o mestrado em Ciência Política no [Instituto Universitário de Pesquisas do Rio de Janeiro](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instituto_Universitário_de_Pesquisas_do_Rio_de_Janeiro "Instituto Universitário de Pesquisas do Rio de Janeiro") (IUPERJ), o atual [Instituto de Estudos Sociais e Políticos](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instituto_de_Estudos_Sociais_e_Políticos "Instituto de Estudos Sociais e Políticos") (IESP), da UERJ, com a dissertação "O Movimento de Favelados do Rio de Janeiro: Políticas do Estado e Lutas Sociais".[[8]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-portal-8)

Ainda na elaboração de sua dissertação, ingressou, em 1987, como pesquisadora na [Casa de Oswaldo Cruz](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casa_de_Oswaldo_Cruz "Casa de Oswaldo Cruz") (COC),[[9]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-COC-9) cuja missão é a pesquisa histórica sobre as ciências e a saúde e como elas são fundamentais para a reflexão crítica sobre a sociedade brasileira. Em 1992, deu início ao [doutorado](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doutoramento "Doutoramento"), também na IUPERJ. Defendida, em 1997, a tese *Um Sertão Chamado Brasil*[[10]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-10) ganhou o Prêmio de Melhor Tese de Doutorado em Sociologia no IUPERJ e foi publicada em livro pela editora da instituição, com uma segunda edição publicada pela Hucitec, em 2013.[[7]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-iesp-7)[[8]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-portal-8)

Foi chefe do departamento de pesquisa da COC (1989–1991), vice-diretora (1992–1994) e diretora da unidade entre 1998 e 2005. Foi membro da equipe de elaboração do projeto do [Museu da Vida](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museu_da_Vida "Museu da Vida"), inaugurado, em 1999. Em 2000, recebeu a Medalha do Centenário da Fundação Oswaldo Cruz (Fiocruz). Como diretora da COC criou o Programa de Pós-graduação em História das Ciências e da Saúde (PPGHCS), em 2000.[[8]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-portal-8)[[11]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-academia-11)

Em dezembro de 2020, foi eleita membra titular da Academia Brasileira de Ciências (ABC)[[12]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-12) na categoria Ciências Sociais. Em 1º de janeiro de 2022, ela se tornou membro da Academia Mundial de Ciências (TWAS)[[13]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-13) para o avanço da ciência nos países em desenvolvimento.

## Carreira acadêmica

Foi pesquisadora de produtividade de nível superior do [Conselho Nacional de Desenvolvimento Científico e Tecnológico (CNPq)](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conselho_Nacional_de_Desenvolvimento_Científico_e_Tecnológico "Conselho Nacional de Desenvolvimento Científico e Tecnológico")[[14]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-fiocruzfiável-14)

No magistério médico atuou em vários níveis de formação, desde o ensino fundamental até o pós-doutorado, tanto na Fiocruz quanto na [Universidade do Estado do Rio de Janeiro](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universidade_do_Estado_do_Rio_de_Janeiro "Universidade do Estado do Rio de Janeiro"). Publicou vários estudos, tanto em livros quanto em artigos e capítulos de obras alheias. Dentre suas realizações está a criação da Biblioteca Virtual do Pensamento Social (BVPS), em parceria com a UERJ e outras instituições, além de integrar conselhos editoriais de periódicos como Revista da Sociedade Brasileira de História da Ciência; História, Ciências, Saúde-Manguinhos; Caderno de História da Ciência-[Instituto Butantan](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instituto_Butantan "Instituto Butantan"); Escritos da [Fundação Casa de Rui Barbosa](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundação_Casa_de_Rui_Barbosa "Fundação Casa de Rui Barbosa") e *Medical History*.[[14]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-fiocruzfiável-14)

### Primeira mulher a presidir a Fiocruz

Primeira mulher a comandar a [Fundação Oswaldo Cruz](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundação_Oswaldo_Cruz "Fundação Oswaldo Cruz") em 120 anos de história da instituição, assumiu a direção da instituição em [4 de janeiro](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_de_janeiro "4 de janeiro") de [2017](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017 "2017"), tendo sido a mais votada na eleição interna.[[15]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-smcrj-15)[[16]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-17)

Durante seu mandato coordenou em 2018 a *Rede Zika Ciências Sociais*, parte da *Zika Alliance Network* com parceria de cinquenta e quatro entidades parceiras no mundo. Trindade Lima integrou programas internacionais de história da ciência e da saúde e ainda em 2018 foi membra de grupo do Plano de Ação Global da [OMS](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organização_Mundial_da_Saúde "Organização Mundial da Saúde") que tem por finalidade otimizar a pesquisa dos sistemas de saúde nos países e, no ano seguinte, integrou o corpo consultivo da OMS para a [Agenda 2030](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Objetivos_de_Desenvolvimento_Sustentável "Objetivos de Desenvolvimento Sustentável"), sendo neste ano co-presidenta da Rede de Saúde para Todos da UNSDSN.[[14]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-fiocruzfiável-14)

### Atuação na pandemia

Durante sua gestão, liderou as ações da Fiocruz no enfrentamento da [pandemia de COVID-19 no Brasil](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandemia_de_COVID-19_no_Brasil "Pandemia de COVID-19 no Brasil"). Dentre as iniciativas, estãoː a criação um novo Centro Hospitalar no *campus* de Manguinhos; coordenação no país do ensaio clínico *Solidarity* da [Organização Mundial da Saúde](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organização_Mundial_da_Saúde "Organização Mundial da Saúde") (OMS); aumento da capacidade nacional de produção de kits de diagnóstico e processamento de resultados de testagens; organização de ações emergenciais junto a populações vulneráveis; oferta de cursos virtuais, para profissionais do [Sistema Único de Saúde](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sistema_Único_de_Saúde "Sistema Único de Saúde") (SUS), de manejo clínico e atenção hospitalar para pacientes de COVID-19; lançamento de manual de biossegurança em escolas; e a Fiocruz tornou-se laboratório de referência para a OMS em COVID-19 nas Américas.[[14]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-fiocruzfiável-14)

Foi responsável pela criação do Observatório COVID-19, rede transdisciplinar que realiza pesquisas e sistematiza dados epidemiológicos; monitora e divulga informações, para subsidiar políticas públicas, sobre a circulação do novo coronavírus e seus impactos sociais em diferentes regiões no Brasil.

Coordenou o acordo de encomenda tecnológica na articulação com o [Ministério da Saúde do Brasil](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministério_da_Saúde_(Brasil) "Ministério da Saúde (Brasil)"), a [Universidade de Oxford](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universidade_de_Oxford "Universidade de Oxford"), a farmacêutica [AstraZeneca](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/AstraZeneca "AstraZeneca") e as unidades de produção locais, para a realização dos testes clínicos, registro sanitário e a produção de milhões de doses da [vacina contra a COVID-19 da AstraZeneca-Oxford no Brasil](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/AZD1222 "AZD1222").

Em [11 de janeiro](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/11_de_janeiro "11 de janeiro") de [2021](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021 "2021"), foi reconduzida ao cargo de presidente da Fiocruz, após ter sido votada em eleição interna, na qual recebeu 87 [por cento](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porcentagem "Porcentagem") dos votos válidos.[[18]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-18)

Em 1 de setembro de 2021, foi condecorada com o grau de Cavaleira da [Ordem Nacional da Legião de Honra](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordem_Nacional_da_Legião_de_Honra "Ordem Nacional da Legião de Honra") (*Ordre National de la Légion d'Honneur*), da [França](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/França "França"), em reconhecimento à atuação da presidente da Fundação nas áreas da Ciência e da Saúde, em particular pelas ações da instituição no enfrentamento da pandemia de COVID-19.[[19]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-19)

## Ministério da Saúde

Em 22 de dezembro de 2022, foi anunciada, pelo presidente eleito [Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luiz_Inácio_Lula_da_Silva "Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva"), para ocupar o cargo de [ministra da Saúde](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministério_da_Saúde_(Brasil) "Ministério da Saúde (Brasil)"), a partir de 1 de janeiro de 2023. Será também, desta forma, a primeira mulher a ocupar o cargo na história do Ministério.[[20]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-20) A escolha foi elogiada pelo diretor-geral da [OMS](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organização_Mundial_da_Saúde "Organização Mundial da Saúde") (Organização Mundial da Saúde), [Tedros Adhanom](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tedros_Adhanom "Tedros Adhanom"), tanto em entrevista coletiva à imprensa[[21]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-21), quanto no perfil oficial mantido por ele no Twitter[[22]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-22).

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/38/14.07.2023_-_Cerim%C3%B4nia_de_San%C3%A7%C3%A3o_do_Novo_Mais_M%C3%A9dicos_%2853046284865%29.jpg/250px-14.07.2023_-_Cerim%C3%B4nia_de_San%C3%A7%C3%A3o_do_Novo_Mais_M%C3%A9dicos_%2853046284865%29.jpg?utm_source=pt.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ficheiro:14.07.2023_-_Cerimônia_de_Sanção_do_Novo_Mais_Médicos_(53046284865).jpg)A Ministra da Saúde, Nísia Trindade, participa da cerimônia de sanção do novo programa Mais Médicos pelo Presidente Lula, em julho de 2023.

Ao assumir oficialmente a pasta em 02 de janeiro, a ministra afirmou, que sua gestão à frente da Saúde seria pautada e pelo diálogo com a comunidade científica. Também anunciou a revogação de decretos e normativas do [Governo Bolsonaro](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governo_Jair_Bolsonaro "Governo Jair Bolsonaro") que, segundo ela, ofendem a ciência, os Direitos Humanos e os direitos reprodutivos.[[23]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-23)

Em junho de 2023, foi admitida pelo presidente Lula à [Ordem do Mérito da Defesa](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordem_do_Mérito_da_Defesa "Ordem do Mérito da Defesa") já em seu último grau, a Grã-Cruz, e em novembro promovida ao mesmo grau na [Ordem de Rio Branco](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordem_de_Rio_Branco "Ordem de Rio Branco").[[24]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-25)

### Crise Humanitária na terra Yanomami

Ver artigo principal: [Crise humanitária ianomâmi em 2022-2023](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crise_humanitária_ianomâmi_em_2022-2023 "Crise humanitária ianomâmi em 2022-2023")

Em 22 de janeiro de 2023, a ministra Nísia Trindade decretou estado de emergência em Saúde Pública na terra indígena [Yanomami](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ianomâmis "Ianomâmis"), localizada no estado de [Roraima](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roraima "Roraima"), por conta da morte de crianças por desnutrição, o alastramento da malária e da contaminação por mercúrio, decorrentes do garimpo ilegal. A medida foi tomada após uma visita da ministra e do Presidente Lula à reserva indígena. Na ocasião, ambos afirmaram haver suspeitas de omissão do governo anterior em relação aos povos indígenas yanomami.[[26]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-26)

### Dengue

Como um dos instrumentos para enfrentar a dengue, Nísia garantiu que o Brasil fosse o primeiro país do mundo a oferecer vacinas no sistema público, tendo adquirido todo o quantitativo disponível das vacinas Qdenga,[[27]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-27)produzidas pela farmacêutica Takeda. Entretanto, esse quantitativo só permitia a aplicação em um grupo-alvo reduzido: crianças e adolescentes de 10 a 14 anos em determinadas regiões. Paralelamente, a fim de garantir uma oferta que permita uma massificação da vacinação, foram intensificadas ações junto ao Instituto Butantan e à Fundação Oswaldo Cruz para a produção de uma vacina própria de dose única[[28]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-28) e de outra a partir da transferência de tecnologia com a Takeda.[[29]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-29)

Em 2024 o número de casos de dengue atingiu o recorde de 6,6 milhões, resultando em pelo menos 6.016 mortes pela doença.[[30]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-30) Na comparação com o ano anterior, o número de casos aumentou em 400% e ultrapassou a quantidade de casos e óbitos decorrentes de [COVID-19](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19") no mesmo período, com 862 mil casos e 5.959 óbitos.[[31]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-32)

### Demissão

Em 25 de fevereiro de 2025, o governo anunciou a demissão de Nísia. No cargo desde o início do governo, Nísia vinha enfrentando pressões para imprimir um viés mais político à pasta e concretizar entregas consideradas prioritárias por Lula.[[33]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-33) Desde o início de 2025, as cobranças se intensificaram em diversas reuniões fechadas entre a ministra e o presidente, no [Palácio do Planalto](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palácio_do_Planalto "Palácio do Planalto"). O entorno de Nísia chegou a reclamar do “abandono” das mulheres do governo e do [PT](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partido_dos_Trabalhadores "Partido dos Trabalhadores") na defesa de sua permanência à frente da pasta, segundo apurou a CNN.[[4]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-:0-4)

O ato de exoneração foi publicado em 10 de março de 2025, sendo [Alexandre Padilha](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandre_Padilha "Alexandre Padilha") nomeado para o cargo de ministro da Saúde.[[34]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-Brasil-35)

## Deputada federal

Nas eleições de 2026, Nísia foi eleita para o cargo de [deputada federal](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputado_federal "Deputado federal") pelo [Rio de Janeiro](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro_(estado) "Rio de Janeiro (estado)"), com 67.350 votos.[[36]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%ADsia_Trindade_Lima#cite_note-36)

Here are all individuals who held the **U.S. Secretary of Transportation** position from **January 1, 2018** through **December 31, 2024**, including short‑acting secretaries:

| # | Name | Type | Took Office | Left Office | President during tenure |

- **Elaine Chao** was in office throughout 2018.
- **Steven G. Bradbury** and **Lana Hurdle** served only briefly in early January 2021 while the office was vacant after Chao’s resignation.
- **Pete Buttigieg** succeeded them and remained Secretary until his scheduled departure at the end of 2024 (Jan 20, 2025).

The **United States secretary of transportation** is the head of the [United States Department of Transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Transportation "United States Department of Transportation"). The secretary serves as the principal advisor to the [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") on all matters relating to transportation. The secretary is a statutory member of the [Cabinet of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States"), and is fourteenth in the [presidential line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_line_of_succession "United States presidential line of succession").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-code-1)

The secretary of transportation oversees the U.S. Department of Transportation, which has over 55,000 employees and [thirteen agencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Transportation#Agencies "United States Department of Transportation"), including the [Federal Aviation Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Aviation_Administration "Federal Aviation Administration"), the [Federal Highway Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Highway_Administration "Federal Highway Administration"), the [Federal Railroad Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Railroad_Administration "Federal Railroad Administration"), and the [National Highway Traffic Safety Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Highway_Traffic_Safety_Administration "National Highway Traffic Safety Administration").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-DOTHist-2) As of January 2021, the secretary receives an annual salary of $221,400.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-Salary-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-4)

[Sean Duffy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Duffy "Sean Duffy") has served as the 20th secretary of transportation since January 28, 2025. He was appointed by President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") to serve this position, and was confirmed by the [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") in a 77-22 vote.

## History

The post was created on October 15, 1966, by the Department of Transportation Act, signed into law by President [Lyndon B. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson "Lyndon B. Johnson").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-DOTHist-2) The department's mission is "to develop and coordinate policies that will provide an efficient and economical national transportation system, with due regard for need, the environment, and the national defense."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-DOTHist-2)

The first secretary of transportation was [Alan S. Boyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_S._Boyd "Alan S. Boyd"), nominated to the post by Democratic president Lyndon B. Johnson. [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan")'s second secretary of transportation, [Elizabeth Dole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Dole "Elizabeth Dole"), was the first female holder, and Mary Peters was the second. [Gerald Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Ford "Gerald Ford")'s nominee [William Thaddeus Coleman Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Thaddeus_Coleman_Jr. "William Thaddeus Coleman Jr.") was the first African American to serve as transportation secretary, and [Federico Peña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federico_Peña "Federico Peña"), serving under [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton"), was the first Hispanic to hold the position, subsequently becoming the [secretary of energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_Energy "Secretary of Energy"). Japanese-American [Norman Mineta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Mineta "Norman Mineta"), who had previously been the [secretary of commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_Commerce "Secretary of Commerce"), is the longest-serving secretary, holding the post for over five and a half years,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-DOTHist-2) and [Andrew Card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Card "Andrew Card") is the shortest-serving secretary, serving only eleven months. [Pete Buttigieg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg "Pete Buttigieg") is the youngest secretary, taking office at 39 years 15 days old, overtaking [Neil Goldschmidt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Goldschmidt "Neil Goldschmidt") as the youngest secretary, taking office at 39 years 3 months old,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-CNBC-5) while Norman Mineta was the oldest, retiring at age 74.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-DOTBio-6) Buttigieg is also the first openly [gay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gay "Gay") man to hold the position, as well as being the first openly gay Cabinet secretary, and the first to seek a full senate confirmation.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-7) In April 2008, [Mary Peters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_E._Peters "Mary E. Peters") launched the official blog of the secretary of transportation called *The Fast Lane*.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-8) On January 23, 2009, the 16th secretary, [Ray LaHood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_LaHood "Ray LaHood"), took office, serving under the administration of Democrat [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama"); he had previously been a Republican congressman from Illinois for fourteen years.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-9)

[Anthony Foxx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Foxx "Anthony Foxx") was the 17th U.S. secretary of transportation from 2013 to 2017, when [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") was president. [Elaine Chao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao "Elaine Chao"), who served as the [secretary of labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Labor "United States Secretary of Labor") under President [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush"), was nominated by [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") on November 29, 2016. On January 31, 2017, the Senate confirmed her appointment by a vote of 93–6. On January 7, 2021, Chao announced her resignation following the [January 6 United States Capitol attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/January_6_United_States_Capitol_attack "January 6 United States Capitol attack"), effective January 11.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-10) On January 11, 2021, acting [deputy secretary of transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Deputy_Secretary_of_Transportation "United States Deputy Secretary of Transportation") [Steven G. Bradbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_G._Bradbury "Steven G. Bradbury") became acting secretary of transportation. Pete Buttigieg served as the 19th secretary of transportation during the presidency of [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden").

**Elaine Lan Chao** (born March 26, 1953) is an American businesswoman and former government official who served as [United States secretary of labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_secretary_of_labor "United States secretary of labor") in the [administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush_administration "George W. Bush administration") of [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush") from 2001 to 2009 and as [United States secretary of transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_secretary_of_transportation "United States secretary of transportation") in the [first administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "First presidency of Donald Trump") of [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") from 2017 to 2021. A member of the [Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") and wife of U.S. senator [Mitch McConnell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitch_McConnell "Mitch McConnell"), Chao was the first [Asian-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_Americans "Asian Americans") woman to serve in a [presidential cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-2) She resigned as secretary of transportation after the [January 6 United States Capitol attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/January_6_United_States_Capitol_attack "January 6 United States Capitol attack").

Born in [Taipei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taipei "Taipei"), [Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan "Taiwan"), Chao immigrated to the United States when she was eight years old. Her father founded the [Foremost Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foremost_Group "Foremost Group"), an American shipping company based in New York. Chao was raised in [Queens, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queens,_New_York "Queens, New York"), and on [Long Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island "Long Island"), and received degrees from [Mount Holyoke College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Holyoke_College "Mount Holyoke College") and [Harvard Business School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Business_School "Harvard Business School"). She worked for financial institutions before being appointed to senior positions in the [Department of Transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Transportation "United States Department of Transportation") under Presidents [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan") and [George H. W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._W._Bush "George H. W. Bush"), including chair of the [Federal Maritime Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Maritime_Commission "Federal Maritime Commission") (1988–1989) and [Deputy Secretary of Transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputy_Secretary_of_Transportation "Deputy Secretary of Transportation") (1989–1991).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-3) She served as director of the [Peace Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_Corps "Peace Corps") from 1991 to 1992 and as president of the [United Way of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Way_of_America "United Way of America") from 1993 to 1996.

Chao has served on several *Fortune* 500 and nonprofit [boards of directors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boards_of_directors "Boards of directors"), including the electric charger network provider [ChargePoint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ChargePoint "ChargePoint") since 2021.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-5)

## Early life and career

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/79/Elaine_Chao_in_1971_Red_%27n%27_White.jpg/250px-Elaine_Chao_in_1971_Red_%27n%27_White.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Elaine_Chao_in_1971_Red_'n'_White.jpg)Chao in [Syosset High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syosset_High_School "Syosset High School")'s yearbook

Elaine Chao was born in [Taipei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taipei "Taipei"), [Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan "Taiwan"), on March 26, 1953, and immigrated to the United States when she was eight years old. She is the eldest of six daughters of [Ruth Mulan Chu Chao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Mulan_Chu_Chao "Ruth Mulan Chu Chao"), a historian from [Anhui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anhui "Anhui"), and [James S. C. Chao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_S._C._Chao "James S. C. Chao"), a [Shanghainese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghainese "Shanghainese") businessman who began his career as a [merchant mariner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merchant_mariner "Merchant mariner") and in 1964 founded the shipping company Foremost Maritime Corporation in New York City, which developed into the [Foremost Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foremost_Group "Foremost Group"). In 1961, at the age of 8, Chao came to the United States on a 37-day freight ship journey along with her mother and two younger sisters. Her father had arrived in New York three years earlier and sent money home until the rest of the family could join him in the United States.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-FTV-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-7)

Chao described her early life in America as a typical immigrant story, noting that "everything was foreign to us: the culture, people, language, traditions, and even the food."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-Flynn-2014-8) She spoke no English upon her arrival.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-9) Her father "worked three jobs" to support the family and the then-five family members lived in a one-bedroom apartment.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-Flynn-2014-8)

### Education

Chao attended Tsai Hsing Elementary School in Taiwan for [kindergarten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kindergarten "Kindergarten") and first grade.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-FTV-6)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-10) She attended [Syosset High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syosset_High_School "Syosset High School") in [Syosset, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syosset,_New_York "Syosset, New York"), in [Nassau County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nassau_County,_New_York "Nassau County, New York") on [Long Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island "Long Island")[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-11) and was [naturalized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naturalized_U.S._citizen "Naturalized U.S. citizen") as a U.S. citizen at the age of 19.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-12)

Chao received a Bachelor of Arts degree in [economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics "Economics") from [Mount Holyoke College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Holyoke_College "Mount Holyoke College") in [South Hadley, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Hadley,_Massachusetts "South Hadley, Massachusetts"). In the second semester of her junior year, she studied at [Dartmouth College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmouth_College "Dartmouth College"). She received an [MBA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBA "MBA") degree from [Harvard Business School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Business_School "Harvard Business School").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-13)

### Early career

Before being appointed to government work, Chao was a vice president for [syndications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syndicated_loan "Syndicated loan") at [Bank of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_America "Bank of America") Capital Markets Group in San Francisco, and she was an international banker at [Citicorp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citicorp "Citicorp") in New York.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-bb-14) She was granted a [White House Fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House_Fellowship "White House Fellowship") during the [Reagan Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reagan_Administration "Reagan Administration").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-15)

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/af/Office_of_the_Assistant_Secretary_for_Administration_and_Management_-_Secretary_Elaine_Chao_Presents_Awards_at_the_2005_Honor_Awards_Ceremony_-_DPLA_-_7b912d5460eb9375a48628bd13d33f48_%28page_287%29_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-thumbnail.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Office_of_the_Assistant_Secretary_for_Administration_and_Management_-_Secretary_Elaine_Chao_Presents_Awards_at_the_2005_Honor_Awards_Ceremony_-_DPLA_-_7b912d5460eb9375a48628bd13d33f48_(page_287)_(cropped).jpg)Chao in 2005

In 1986, Chao became Deputy Administrator of the [Maritime Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Maritime_Administration "United States Maritime Administration") in the [U.S. Department of Transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Department_of_Transportation "U.S. Department of Transportation"). From 1988 to 1989, she served as chairwoman of the [Federal Maritime Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Maritime_Commission "Federal Maritime Commission").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-bio-16) In 1989, then-president George H.W. Bush nominated Chao to be Deputy Secretary of Transportation; she served from 1989 to 1991.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-picks-17) From 1991 to 1992, she was the director of the Peace Corps.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-bio-16) She was the first [Asian American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_American "Asian American") to serve in any of these positions. She expanded the Peace Corps' presence in Eastern Europe and Central Asia by establishing the first Peace Corps programs in [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland "Poland"), [Latvia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latvia "Latvia"), [Lithuania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithuania "Lithuania"), [Estonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estonia "Estonia"), and the newly independent states of the former [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union"), including the first Peace Corps programs in Ukraine, Georgia, Armenia and Russia.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-19)

## Between Bush administrations

Following her service in President George H.W. Bush's administration, Chao worked from 1992 to 1996 as president and CEO of United Way of America.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-21) She was the first Asian American to hold that role. She is credited with returning credibility and public trust to the organization after a financial mismanagement scandal involving former president [William Aramony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Aramony "William Aramony").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-22) From 1996 until her appointment as Secretary of Labor, Chao worked at a [conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservatism_in_the_United_States "Conservatism in the United States") [think tank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Think_tank "Think tank") in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.")[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-23) She was also a board member of the [Independent Women's Forum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_Women's_Forum "Independent Women's Forum").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-ronnee-24) She later returned to think tanks after leaving the government in January 2009.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-know-25)

Chao delivered a speech at the [2000 Republican National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Republican_National_Convention "2000 Republican National Convention").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-26)

## U.S. Secretary of Labor (2001–2009)

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b1/Elaine_Chao_large.jpg/250px-Elaine_Chao_large.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Elaine_Chao_large.jpg)Official Secretary of Labor photo

Chao was the only cabinet member in the [George W. Bush administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush_administration "George W. Bush administration") to serve for the entirety of his eight years.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-27) She was also the longest-serving Secretary of Labor since [Frances Perkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frances_Perkins "Frances Perkins"), who served from 1933 to 1945 under President [Franklin D. Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt "Franklin D. Roosevelt").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-28) Chao was unanimously confirmed by the Senate for her appointment as Secretary of Labor.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-29) Of Chao's staff, [Victoria Lipnic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Lipnic "Victoria Lipnic"), Assistant Secretary for Employment Standards Administration, later became Member, EEOC and acting chair.

In 2002, the Bush administration obtained a national emergency [injunction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Injunction "Injunction") to end an employers' lockout of unionized dockworkers on the West Coast, invoking the [Taft–Hartley Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taft–Hartley_Act "Taft–Hartley Act") for the first time since 1971 after Chao had been unable to negotiate a new contract between the employers and the union in a dispute over the use of new technology.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-31)

In 2004, the department issued revisions of the white-collar overtime regulations under the [Fair Labor Standards Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fair_Labor_Standards_Act "Fair Labor Standards Act").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-32)

### Union pension plan and trust disclosure requirements

In 2003, the department updated the labor union financial disclosure regulations under the [Landrum–Griffin Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landrum–Griffin_Act "Landrum–Griffin Act") of 1959, requiring more extensive disclosures for union-sponsored pension plans and union-related trusts such as strike funds.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-34)

### Response to 9/11, Hurricane Katrina

Following the [terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrorist_attacks_of_September_11,_2001 "Terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001"), Chao's Department of Labor disbursed grants to provide temporary jobs to assist in cleanup and restoration efforts in New York, as well as the Occupational Safety and Health Administration's monitoring of health and safety of [cleanup work](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rescue_and_recovery_effort_after_the_September_11_attacks_on_the_World_Trade_Center "Rescue and recovery effort after the September 11 attacks on the World Trade Center") being performed at the disaster sites including lower Manhattan. The department also provided unemployment insurance and income support to those who lost their jobs in the aftermath of September 11.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-MassTransit-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-37)

Following the 2005 hurricane season, which included hurricanes [Katrina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Katrina "Hurricane Katrina"), [Rita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Rita "Hurricane Rita") and [Wilma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Wilma "Hurricane Wilma"), the Labor Department disbursed nearly $380 million in grants to assist with cleanup work and provide benefits and services to those displaced by the storms. The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) and other agencies deployed personnel to the region to provide safety training and uphold workers' rights. Chao set up an emergency response hotline dedicated to the Gulf Coast region for people seeking benefits and worker protection information.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-MassTransit-36)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-38) The suspension of the [Davis–Bacon Act of 1931](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davis–Bacon_Act_of_1931 "Davis–Bacon Act of 1931") and OSHA protections in the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina has been linked to the exploitation of illegal immigrant workers in New Orleans, who often worked without protective gear in hazardous conditions and were underpaid[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-40)

### Government Accountability Office reports

After analyzing 70,000 closed case files from 2005 to 2007, the [Government Accountability Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_Accountability_Office "Government Accountability Office") reported that the Department's [Wage and Hour Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wage_and_Hour_Division "Wage and Hour Division") (WHD) inadequately investigated complaints from low- and [minimum-wage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_wage_in_the_United_States "Minimum wage in the United States") workers alleging that employers failed to pay the [federal minimum wage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_wage_in_the_United_States "Minimum wage in the United States"), required overtime, and failed to issue a last paycheck.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-42) The Department of Labor responded that the GAO investigation focused on individual complaints while the department remained focused on resolving complex and multi-employee complaints; from 1997 to 2007 the annual number of employees receiving back wages as a result of DOL action almost doubled and the dollar amount of back wages paid more than doubled.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-43) *[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post "The Washington Post")* echoed that Chao's department was criticized by some for "walking away from its regulatory function" but also praised by others for providing "compliance assistance" and "helping companies abide by the law" rather than "punitive enforcement that ... stifles economic growth."[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-Fletcher-44)

A 2008 [Government Accountability Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_Accountability_Office "Government Accountability Office") report noted that the Labor Department gave Congress inaccurate numbers which understated the expense of contracting out its employees' work to private firms during Chao's tenure, which may have affected 22 employees at the department.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-WashP-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-46)

### Mining regulation

Chao and the Bush administration proposed quadrupling the fines imposed against mining corporations for mine safety breaches and sued mine operators for failing to maintain safe working conditions.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-Gainesville-47) A 2007 report by the department's [Office of Inspector General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_inspector_general_(United_States) "Office of inspector general (United States)") (OIG) found that mine safety regulators did not conduct federally required inspections at more than one in seven of the country's 731 underground coal mines in 2006, and that the number of worker deaths in mining accidents more than doubled to 47 in that year.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-hsu-48)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-Fletcher-44)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-49) The [Mine Safety and Health Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mine_Safety_and_Health_Administration "Mine Safety and Health Administration") (MSHA) "missed 147 inspections at 107 mines employing a total of 7,500 workers".[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-hsu-48)

Mining disasters in 2006 and 2007 included West Virginia's [Sago Mine explosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sago_Mine_disaster "Sago Mine disaster"), which killed 12 in January 2006;[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-hsu-48) West Virginia's [Alma Mine fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aracoma_Alma_Mine_accident "Aracoma Alma Mine accident"), which killed two in January 2006;[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-victory-50) the [Darby Mine No. 1 explosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darby_Mine_No._1_disaster "Darby Mine No. 1 disaster") in Kentucky, where five miners died in May 2006;[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-hsu-48) and the [Crandall Canyon Mine collapse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crandall_Canyon_Mine "Crandall Canyon Mine") in Utah, which killed six workers and three rescuers in August 2007.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-hsu-48) Immediately following the Sago mine disaster, Secretary Chao vowed to "take the necessary steps to ensure that this never happens again".[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-Gainesville-47)

In 2010, the widows of the two men killed in the Alma Mine fire sued the federal government for wrongful death, citing lack of inspections, failure to act against violations, and conflicts of interest.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-jj140929-52) "MSHA's review of the fire acknowledged significant lapses by inspectors, supervisors and district managers" at the mine but the agency did not admit liability for the negligent inspections.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-MSAH_settles-54) In 2013, the appeals court ruled that MSHA can be held liable "when a negligent inspection results in the wrongful death of a coal miner".[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-MSAH_settles-54) The suit was settled in 2014; MSHA also agreed to develop a training course on preventing fires in underground mines.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-jj140929-52)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-MSAH_settles-54)

### Workplace safety

A 2009 inspector general report evaluating an [Occupational Safety and Health Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupational_Safety_and_Health_Administration "Occupational Safety and Health Administration") (OSHA) initiative on problematic workplaces for the prior six years found that OSHA, a regulatory agency within the Department of Labor, had failed to gather needed data, conducted uneven inspections and enforcement, and failed to record all fatalities because company names were misspelled or did not account for when companies shared the same owner. The audit also noted that after rules changes in January 2008 the number of targeted companies declined by almost half.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-55) In the opinion of [FreightWaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FreightWaves?action=edit&redlink=1 "FreightWaves (page does not exist)"), a price reporting agency for the global freight market, during Chao's tenure the Department of Labor achieved "record low worker injury, illness and fatality rates; record back wages recovered; [and] record monetary recoveries for workers' pension plans".[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-56)

## Post-Bush administration (2009–2017)

In 2009, Chao resumed her previous role at a think tank,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-know-25) and she contributed to [Fox News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_News "Fox News") and other media outlets.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-57)

She also served as a director on a number of corporate and non-profit boards,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-bb-14)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-cepr-58) including the [Institute of Politics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Institute_of_Politics "Harvard Institute of Politics") at [Harvard Kennedy School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Kennedy_School "Harvard Kennedy School"), [Wells Fargo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Fargo "Wells Fargo"),[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-59) [New York–Presbyterian Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York–Presbyterian_Hospital "New York–Presbyterian Hospital"), [News Corp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News_Corp "News Corp"), [Dole Food Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dole_Food_Company "Dole Food Company"),[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-60) and [Protective Life Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protective_Life_Corporation "Protective Life Corporation").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-63) According to financial disclosure forms, Chao was slated to receive $1–5 million as compensation for her service on the board of Wells Fargo.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-64) In June 2011, she was awarded the [Woodrow Wilson Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodrow_Wilson_Award "Woodrow Wilson Award") for Public Service.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-65)

In January 2015, she resigned from the board of [Bloomberg Philanthropies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomberg_Philanthropies "Bloomberg Philanthropies"), which she had joined in 2012,[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-66) because of its plans to significantly increase support for the [Sierra Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Club "Sierra Club")'s "[Beyond Coal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beyond_Coal "Beyond Coal")" initiative.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-67)

In February 2017, the [Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press "Associated Press") reported that Chao was paid by a speaker's bureau to give a speech regarding women's empowerment to an organization later found to be linked to the [People's Mujahedin of Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Mujahedin_of_Iran "People's Mujahedin of Iran") (aka Mojahedin-e Khalq or MEK), a group exiled from Iran after actions in the 1970s against the Shah of Iran and the Ayatollah Khomeini. Similar speeches were delivered by former Joint Chiefs of Staff General [Hugh Shelton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Shelton "Hugh Shelton"), Commandant of the U.S. Marine Corps General [James T. Conway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_T._Conway "James T. Conway"), former National Security Advisor General [James L. Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_L._Jones "James L. Jones"), former CIA Directors [Porter Goss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porter_Goss "Porter Goss") and [James Woolsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Woolsey "James Woolsey"), former FBI Director [Louis Freeh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Freeh "Louis Freeh"), former [NYC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NYC "NYC") Mayor [Rudy Giuliani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudy_Giuliani "Rudy Giuliani"), and former Governors [Howard Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Dean "Howard Dean") of Vermont and [Ed Rendell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Rendell "Ed Rendell") of Pennsylvania.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-69)

## U.S. Secretary of Transportation (2017–2021)

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/Elaine_Chao_at_confirmation_hearing.jpg/250px-Elaine_Chao_at_confirmation_hearing.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Elaine_Chao_at_confirmation_hearing.jpg)Chao at her confirmation hearing to be Secretary of Transportation

U.S. President-elect Donald Trump announced on November 29, 2016, that he would nominate Chao to be Secretary of Transportation.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-picks-17) The U.S. Senate confirmed Chao on January 31, 2017, by a vote of 93–6, with her husband, then-Senate majority leader [Mitch McConnell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitch_McConnell "Mitch McConnell"), abstaining.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-TransportVote-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_2017-71)

As Secretary of Transportation, Chao led the presidential delegation to the enthronement ceremony for [Japanese emperor Naruhito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naruhito "Naruhito").[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-72) She led the U.S. delegation to the inauguration of Indonesia's President [Joko Widodo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joko_Widodo "Joko Widodo").[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-73)

### Drone technology

In 2017, Chao announced the establishment of a pilot program to test and evaluate the integration of civil and public drone operations into the airspace system.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-Commercial_UAV_News_2017-74) In 2018, ten applicants were selected to participate in the project.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-Avionics_2018-75) In 2019, the [Federal Aviation Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Aviation_Administration "Federal Aviation Administration") (FAA) issued an air carrier and operator certificate to [UPS Flight Forward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UPS_Flight_Forward "UPS Flight Forward") for drone deliveries to a hospital campus in Raleigh, North Carolina.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-CBS_News_2019-76) In December 2019, after multiple reports in Colorado and Nebraska of unidentified objects flying in formation at night over several remote rural counties, the FAA proposed a new rule that would require drones to be remotely identifiable.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-Condon_2020-77)

[Jeffrey A. Rosen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffrey_A._Rosen "Jeffrey A. Rosen") chaired Chao's New and Emerging Technologies Council (NETT)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-78) Chao and Rosen led DOTs efforts to safely enable the use of drones in the airspace, including in FAA's drone pilot program.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-79) The DOT under Chao issued updated guidelines on automated or "self-driving" cars and trucks.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-80) He also helped with FAA's successful efforts to reform its regulations and restore the US lead in enabling the largest number of private commercial space launches.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-81)

Under Chao, Rosen served as Chair of DOT's Regulatory Reform Task Force.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-82) He and Chao focused on improving the infrastructure permitting process, and reforming the regulatory system to reduce costs.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-83)

### COVID-19 responses

In May 2020, following the start of the [COVID-19 outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_outbreak "COVID-19 outbreak") and related changes to travel, Chao sternly warned airlines to follow their published ticket refund procedures, as well as DOT regulations, in light of high demand for travel changes.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-Josephs-2020-84) She demanded airlines provide cash refunds (as opposed to vouchers) when required by law, and urged them to provide cash refunds as broadly as possible.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-Josephs-2020-84)

Chao later announced the disbursement of $1.2 billion in grants to airports to maintain readiness for when passenger travel returned. The funds were distributed to 405 airports for infrastructure and safety improvements, such as improved runway lighting.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-85) Eight tribal governments were also awarded separate transportation funds to maintain infrastructure during COVID.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-86)

Chao also worked to permit truckers to deliver essential goods to New York City, which had been attempting to impose a 14-day quarantine on out-of-state truckers bringing goods into the city. The city dropped the requirement following federal government pressure.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-87) Her department also worked with state governments to maintain access to highway rest areas, including permitting food trucks to provide hot food to truckers and travelers.

The CARES Act enabled the Department of Transportation to make $114 billion of federal aid available for the transportation sector. The largest allocation was $25 billion to support local public transit systems, of which $22.7 billion was dedicated to large and small urban areas and the remaining $2.2 billion for rural areas. The Act also made available $10 billion for grants to commercial and general aviation airports for capital expenditures, operating expenses such as payroll and utilities, and debt payments; and a $1.02 billion allocation for grants to Amtrak to cover lost revenues, buy fuel and construction materials, and maintain its route network. The CARES Act also enabled the department to provide assistance to the aviation sector through loans and loan guarantees and grants for worker and contractor pay and benefits.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-88)

### Other proposals

In March 2019, Chao announced the formation of the Non-Traditional and Emerging Transportation Technology (NETT) Council, an internal Department of Transportation group for identifying "jurisdictional and regulatory gaps" when considering new transportation technologies.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-Laris_2019-89) In April 2019, the FAA released proposed new regulations to modernize the rules for commercial space flight launches and reentries. At a congressional hearing in July 2019, the president of the [Commercial Spaceflight Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_Spaceflight_Federation "Commercial Spaceflight Federation") criticized the proposal as not delivering on its stated goals.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-90)

In October 2019, Chao launched the Rural Opportunities to Use Transportation for Economic Success (ROUTES) initiative, intended to improve rural transportation infrastructure. It sought to achieve this goal by developing tools and information, aggregating DOT resources, and providing technical assistance. The program is intended to consider the unique needs of rural transportation networks to meet national goals of safety, mobility, and economic competitiveness.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-91)

The US Department of Transportation reportedly sought to cut funding and loan guarantees for domestic American shipping companies, shipyards, and shipbuilders. These proposed budget cuts were rejected by Congress.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-bridge-92) Chao's Department also sought for three years to prevent funding for a program that supports the viability of small domestic US shipyards, and a separate program that issues loan guarantees for the construction or reconstruction of ships with American registration.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-bridge-92)

### Resignation

On January 7, 2021, the day after the [January 6 United States Capitol attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/January_6_United_States_Capitol_attack "January 6 United States Capitol attack"), Chao submitted her resignation effective January 11, 2021. She was then the highest-ranking member of the administration to resign due to the riots and the first cabinet officer to do so; her resignation cited the "traumatic and entirely avoidable" violence and stated that it "deeply troubled" her.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-93)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-94)

After Chao's resignation, Trump referred to her with a racial slur and called the Taiwan-born US citizen a "China lover".[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-95) The slur was immediately condemned by Republicans and Democrats as well as Asian-American organizations and other community leaders, including the CEO of the [Anti-Defamation League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Defamation_League "Anti-Defamation League").[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-96)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-97) Trump also referred to Chao as "crazy".[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-98)[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao#cite_note-99)

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Elaine_Chao_by_Gage_Skidmore.jpg/250px-Elaine_Chao_by_Gage_Skidmore.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Elaine_Chao_by_Gage_Skidmore.jpg)Chao speaking at an event in June 2022
